OffByOneRange.code:
import logging, sys
logging.basicConfig(level=logging.DEBUG, stream=sys.stdout, format='%(levelname)s - %(message)s')
def factorial(n):
    logging.debug('Start of factorial(%s)', n)
    total = 1
    for i in range(n + 1):
        total *= i
        logging.debug('i is %s, total is %s', i, total)
    logging.debug('End of factorial(%s)', n)
    return total

print(factorial(3))
OffByOneRange.caption: Each row is one pass of the loop, with i and total after total *= i has run. The first pass multiplies by 0, and total stays 0 from then on.

playground.label: Logging and assertions (uses input)
playground.code:
import logging, sys
logging.basicConfig(level=logging.DEBUG, stream=sys.stdout, format='%(levelname)s - %(message)s')
def factorial(n):
    total = 1
    for i in range(n + 1):
        total *= i
        logging.debug('i is %s, total is %s', i, total)
    return total
print(factorial(int(input('n: '))))

findings: Chapter 5 of the 3rd edition teaches four ways to find and prevent bugs: raising an exception with the raise statement and catching it with except, assertions that check a condition the programmer believes is true, the logging module with its five levels and its options for a file and for switching messages off, and the debugger of the Mu editor with its Continue, Step In, Step Over, Step Out and Stop controls and its breakpoints, closing with a buggy adding program, a coin flip program and the practice program Buggy Coin Toss Game.

The chapter's printed behaviours reproduce under Python 3.14.4: box_print raises the messages the chapter shows for a width of 1 and a two-character symbol, a failing assert raises AssertionError with an empty message, the level names carry the numbers 10, 20, 30, 40 and 50, the factorial with range(n + 1) returns 0 and the fixed one 120, and the adding program prints 5342 instead of 50 until its answers are converted with int.

The chapter's advice that assertions are for programmer errors follows from how the interpreter treats them: assert expression is equivalent to raising AssertionError only when __debug__ is true, and a program run with the -O option, or code compiled with optimisation, contains no assertion at all, so an assert must never carry a check the program needs to perform on user input.

The chapter presents logging as a replacement for print calls, and the documentation adds what makes it more than that: the default level is WARNING so debug and info calls print nothing until basicConfig lowers the threshold, basicConfig does nothing when the root logger already has handlers unless force=True is given, logging.disable(level) silences that level and every lower one until it is called with NOTSET, and a call that passes arguments to the message formats them only if the message is emitted.

The debugger the chapter describes belongs to the Mu editor, whose five controls correspond to commands of the standard library debugger pdb - step, next, return, continue and break - so the same technique is available in any Python installation, and since Python 3.7 a program can start it with the built-in breakpoint(), which calls sys.breakpointhook and is switched off by setting PYTHONBREAKPOINT to 0.

For an advanced course, chapter 5 is best taught as a choice among four instruments by the question asked: raise when the caller can do something about the error, assert when the programmer's belief must hold, log when the run must leave a record, and step through with the debugger when the state at one point is the question; the chapter's printed outputs hold under 3.14.4, and optimised mode, lazy formatting, force=True, breakpoint(), remote attachment, fine-grained tracebacks and exception notes are what the chapter leaves for the course to add.

Python 3.14 added to debugging a safe way to attach the debugger to a running process, python -m pdb -p followed by the process identifier, built on sys.remote_exec of PEP 768, and lets a hardcoded breakpoint() reuse the last debugger instance so that its breakpoints and settings persist between stops.

Since Python 3.11 a traceback points at the failing expression inside a line with carets, so the failing subscript in a chained lookup can be seen without a debugger, and any exception can carry notes added with add_note, which are printed after the traceback and kept in __notes__, so code that catches and re-raises can say where in the work the error occurred.
title: Debugging for an advanced course: chapter 5 of the 3rd edition and today's Python

nodes.label: Error signalling
nodes.body: Raising Exceptions and the traceback that an unhandled exception prints are how a program says that something went wrong (Sweigart, 2025).

nodes.label: Raising
nodes.body: Raising Exceptions shows how a function refuses a call it cannot serve and how the caller recovers (Sweigart, 2025).

nodes.label: Raise statement
nodes.body: The chapter's box_print() function raises Exception with a message when the symbol is not a single character or the width or height is not greater than 2, and the messages are the ones the chapter shows: 'Width must be greater than 2.' and 'Symbol must be a single character string.' (Sweigart, 2025).
nodes.definition: A raise statement stops the running code and passes an exception to the nearest matching except clause, which is how a function tells its caller that a call was invalid.

nodes.label: Exception message
nodes.body: The except clause of the chapter stores the exception with as err and prints str(err) after 'An exception happened: ', and the message given to the exception is kept in its args (Sweigart, 2025) (Python Software Foundation, 2026).
nodes.definition: The text passed to an exception is kept in its args and printed by str, so an except clause can show a message written for the user instead of a traceback.

nodes.label: Tracebacks
nodes.body: Tracebacks are the record of where an exception passed on its way out (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

nodes.label: Exception unwinding
nodes.body: An exception that is not handled in read_age leaves it, then load, then process, and is caught by the try around the call to process, where the message is invalid literal for int() with base 10: 'abc'; with no handler the same climb ends the program with a traceback (Python Software Foundation, 2026).
nodes.definition: An exception that no function handles leaves each function in turn, up the call stack, until an except clause matches it or the program ends with a traceback.

nodes.label: Traceback reading
nodes.body: A traceback lists the calls from the outermost to the one that raised, each with its file, line, function and source line, then the exception class and message (Python Software Foundation, 2026).
nodes.definition: A traceback lists the calls from the outermost to the one that raised, each with file, line, function and source line, and ends with the exception class and message.

nodes.label: Fine grained locations
nodes.body: Since Python 3.11 a traceback underlines the failing part of the source line with tildes and carets, so for print(data['a']['b']['c']) the marks lie under the last subscript, which raises TypeError: 'NoneType' object is not subscriptable (Galindo Salgado et al., 2021).
nodes.definition: Since Python 3.11 a traceback marks the failing part of a line, so which subscript or call failed in a chained expression can be read from it.

nodes.label: Exception notes
nodes.body: An exception can be given notes with add_note, which are stored in __notes__, so an except clause that re-raises can add where in the work the error occurred, as ['while reading the age field'] (Hatfield-Dodds, 2021) (Python Software Foundation, 2026).
nodes.definition: An exception can carry notes added with add_note, kept in __notes__ and printed after the traceback, so code that re-raises can add context.

nodes.label: Assertion
nodes.body: Assertions are the sanity checks of Chapter 5, meant for errors of the programmer and not of the user (Sweigart, 2025).

nodes.label: Assert
nodes.body: An assertion states what must be true at a point in a program (Sweigart, 2025).

nodes.label: Assert statement
nodes.body: An assert statement consists of the keyword, a condition, and optionally a message; if the condition is false it raises AssertionError, as assert ages[0] <= ages[-1] does when the list was reversed instead of sorted (Sweigart, 2025).
nodes.definition: An assert statement checks a condition the programmer believes is true and raises AssertionError when it is false.

nodes.label: Assertion failure
nodes.body: A failed assert raises AssertionError, a subclass of Exception, whose message is empty when none was given; the chapter's advice is not to catch it with try and except, since the program should stop and be fixed (Sweigart, 2025).
nodes.definition: A failed assertion is an ordinary exception of class AssertionError; the chapter advises against catching it, since it reports a programmer error.

nodes.label: Assert message
nodes.body: The second expression of an assert statement is evaluated only when the condition is false and becomes the message of the AssertionError, as 'x must be positive, got -1' (Python Software Foundation, 2026).
nodes.example: assert x > 0, f'x must be positive, got {x}'
nodes.definition: An assert statement can carry a second expression, evaluated only on failure, whose text becomes the message of the AssertionError.

nodes.label: Assert versus raise
nodes.body: The chapter separates errors of the user, which are handled with exceptions, from errors of the programmer, which are checked with assertions; the reference defines assert as equivalent to raising AssertionError only when __debug__ is true (Sweigart, 2025) (Python Software Foundation, 2026).
nodes.definition: An error the user can cause is checked with an if and a raise; an assert states what must be true if the program is correct.

nodes.label: Optimised mode
nodes.body: Code compiled with optimisation, as under the -O option, contains no assert statements, so exec of compile(src, 'x', 'exec', optimize=1) reaches the line after assert False and prints reached, while a normal run raises; the chapter does not cover this (Python Software Foundation, 2026).
nodes.definition: Under the -O option, and in code compiled with optimisation, assert statements produce no code at all, so a check that must always run is not written as an assertion.

nodes.label: Logging
nodes.body: Logging leaves a record of what a program did, without stopping it (Sweigart, 2025).

nodes.label: Setup
nodes.body: Setting up logging means choosing a threshold, a format and a destination (Sweigart, 2025).

nodes.label: Basic config
nodes.body: logging.basicConfig(level=logging.DEBUG, format='%(asctime)s - %(levelname)s - %(message)s') is the chapter's setup call, placed after import logging at the top of the program (Sweigart, 2025).
nodes.definition: basicConfig sets the threshold, the format and the destination of the root logger; the chapter calls it once at the top of a program.

nodes.label: Log format
nodes.body: The format string names the fields of each line, and the chapter's %(asctime)s - %(levelname)s - %(message)s prints the time, the level and the message separated by dashes (Sweigart, 2025).
nodes.definition: A format string with named fields decides what each log line shows; the chapter's shows time, level and message.

nodes.label: Log to file
nodes.body: Passing filename='myProgramLog.txt' to basicConfig writes the messages to that file, so with the format '%(levelname)s - %(message)s' it holds the lines DEBUG - to the file and CRITICAL - also to the file (Sweigart, 2025).
nodes.definition: Passing filename to basicConfig sends the messages to a text file instead of the screen.

nodes.label: Force reconfigure
nodes.body: basicConfig does nothing if the root logger already has handlers, so a second call with another level is ignored and force=True is needed to replace the first; the chapter does not mention this (Python Software Foundation, 2026).
nodes.definition: basicConfig does nothing if the root logger already has handlers, so a second call is ignored unless force=True is passed.

nodes.label: Levels
nodes.body: Logging levels let one program produce much or little output (Sweigart, 2025).

nodes.label: Logging levels
nodes.body: The five levels are DEBUG, INFO, WARNING, ERROR and CRITICAL, called with logging.debug(), logging.info(), logging.warning(), logging.error() and logging.critical(), and they have the numbers 10, 20, 30, 40 and 50 (Sweigart, 2025) (Python Software Foundation, 2026).
nodes.definition: The five levels run from lowest to highest importance, and each has a number: 10, 20, 30, 40 and 50.

nodes.label: Level threshold
nodes.body: Setting the level in basicConfig to INFO hides the DEBUG messages and shows the others, so raising the threshold removes output without editing the program (Sweigart, 2025).
nodes.definition: A message is shown only if its level is at least the threshold, so raising the threshold hides the lower levels without deleting any call.

nodes.label: Default level
nodes.body: Without basicConfig the root logger's threshold is WARNING, so logging.debug and logging.info print nothing and logging.warning and logging.error print WARNING:root:w and ERROR:root:e to standard error (Python Software Foundation, 2026).
nodes.definition: Without basicConfig the threshold is WARNING, so debug and info calls print nothing and warning and error calls print to standard error.

nodes.label: Disabling logging
nodes.body: logging.disable(logging.CRITICAL) at the top of the program silences every message, and logging.disable(logging.NOTSET) restores them (Sweigart, 2025) (Python Software Foundation, 2026).
nodes.definition: logging.disable silences the given level and all below it; disabling CRITICAL turns every message off, and NOTSET turns them back on.

nodes.label: Practice
nodes.body: Practice in logging is choosing between it and print, and writing the calls well (Sweigart, 2025).

nodes.label: Logging versus print
nodes.body: Practice question 8 asks why logging messages are better than print() for the same message, and the chapter's answer is that log messages are for the programmer while messages the user should see, such as File not found, use print(); its own examples add that one call, logging.disable(logging.CRITICAL), turns every log message off where print calls would each have to be removed (Sweigart, 2025).
nodes.definition: Log messages are for the programmer and print is for the user; log calls stay in the program and one setting switches them all off, where print calls would each have to be deleted.

nodes.label: Lazy formatting
nodes.body: A call such as log.debug('value is %s', obj) formats the message only if it is emitted, so with the level at INFO the object's __str__ runs zero times, while an f-string builds the text first and runs it once; the chapter does not cover this (Python Software Foundation, 2026).
nodes.definition: A message given arguments is formatted only when it is emitted, so a disabled debug call costs no string conversion, unlike an f-string built before the call.

nodes.label: Debugger
nodes.body: The debugger is the fourth instrument, and the one for a question about the state at one line (Sweigart, 2025).

nodes.label: Controls
nodes.body: The chapter names five controls of the Mu debugger and the breakpoint they work with (Sweigart, 2025).

nodes.label: Breakpoint
nodes.body: A breakpoint is set by clicking a line number, which shows a red dot, and the debugger pauses when the program reaches that line; clicking again removes it, and the Inspector pane shows the values of the variables (Sweigart, 2025).
nodes.example: a red dot at a line number
nodes.definition: A breakpoint marks a line at which the debugger pauses the running program so its variables can be read.

nodes.label: Continue control
nodes.body: Continue runs the program until it reaches a breakpoint or ends (Sweigart, 2025).
nodes.definition: Continue runs the program until the next breakpoint or the end.

nodes.label: Step in
nodes.body: Step In executes the next line and, if the line calls a function, moves into that function (Sweigart, 2025).
nodes.definition: Step In executes the next line and, if that line is a call, pauses on the first line of the called function.

nodes.label: Step over
nodes.body: Step Over executes the next line, running any function it calls at full speed without stepping into it (Sweigart, 2025).
nodes.definition: Step Over executes the next line as a whole, running a called function without pausing inside it.

nodes.label: Step out
nodes.body: Step Out executes lines at full speed until the debugger returns from the current function (Sweigart, 2025).
nodes.definition: Step Out runs the rest of the current function and pauses back in the caller.

nodes.label: Python debugger
nodes.body: The standard library has its own debugger, so the technique does not depend on one editor (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

nodes.label: Breakpoint function
nodes.body: Since Python 3.7 the built-in breakpoint() calls sys.breakpointhook, which starts pdb, and setting PYTHONBREAKPOINT to 0 makes the call do nothing, so 'the program went on' prints (Warsaw, 2017) (Python Software Foundation, 2026).
nodes.definition: The built-in breakpoint() pauses the program in the debugger at that line; it calls sys.breakpointhook, and PYTHONBREAKPOINT=0 makes it do nothing.

nodes.label: Pdb commands
nodes.body: pdb has the commands step, next, return, continue, break and where, which correspond to Step In, Step Over, Step Out, Continue, a breakpoint and the call stack (Python Software Foundation, 2026).
nodes.example: step, next, return, continue, break, where
nodes.definition: The standard debugger pdb offers the chapter's controls as commands: step, next, return, continue and break, and where lists the call stack.

io.code: [c for c in ('do_step','do_next','do_return','do_continue','do_break','do_where') if hasattr(__import__('pdb').Pdb, c)]

nodes.label: Remote attach
nodes.body: Python 3.14 lets pdb attach to a running process with python -m pdb -p and its identifier, using sys.remote_exec, and a hardcoded breakpoint() reuses the last debugger instance (Galindo Salgado, Wozniski and Stojanovic, 2024) (Python Software Foundation, 2026).
nodes.definition: Since Python 3.14 the debugger can attach to a running process by its identifier, using sys.remote_exec.

nodes.label: Modern practice
nodes.body: The chapter's worked programs show which instrument finds which kind of bug (Sweigart, 2025).

nodes.label: Worked cases
nodes.body: Three bugs of the chapter's programs are found with logging or the debugger (Sweigart, 2025).

nodes.label: Off by one range
nodes.body: The chapter's factorial loops over range(n + 1), so the first pass multiplies by 0 and factorial(5) returns 0; the log shows i is 0, total is 0, and range(1, n + 1) gives 120 (Sweigart, 2025).
nodes.definition: The chapter's factorial multiplies by zero because its range starts at 0; the log shows i as 0 and total as 0 on the first pass, and range(1, n + 1) fixes it.

nodes.label: String concatenation
nodes.body: The buggy adding program stores '5', '3' and '42' as strings, so the program prints The sum is 5342 where 50 is intended (Sweigart, 2025).
nodes.definition: input and a list of typed answers give strings, and adding strings joins them, so the sum prints as 5342 until each answer is converted with int.

nodes.label: Type mismatch comparison
nodes.body: The Buggy Coin Toss Game asks for 'heads' or 'tails' and then tests toss == guess, where toss is the integer from random.randint(0, 1), so the comparison is always false and no guess is ever right (Sweigart, 2025).
nodes.definition: A number never equals a string, so comparing the integer from randint with 'heads' is always false and the game reports every guess as wrong.

lecture.title: Chapter 5: Debugging
lecture.say: Welcome. Chapter 5 of the book (Sweigart, 2025) is about bugs: how a program tells you it has met one, how you make it tell you sooner, and how you stop it in the middle and look. The chapter page has the same diagrams, and its Lecture tab carries this talk track.

lecture.title: The program runs, the answer is wrong
lecture.say: Begin with the feeling everyone has had: the program does not crash, it just gives the wrong answer. Two of this chapter’s own programs do exactly that, a factorial that returns 0 and an adding program that prints 5342 when it should print 50.

lecture.title: Four instruments, and what surrounds them
lecture.say: This is the map of the chapter, drawn from the chapter’s ontology; it is the same tree the interactive page uses. Error signalling covers raising exceptions and reading the traceback. Assertion covers assert and, importantly, when it is switched off. Logging covers setting it up, the levels and good practice. Debugger covers the controls and the standard library’s own debugger. Modern practice holds the three bugs the chapter’s programs contain. By the end you should be able to say which instrument a given problem calls for.

lecture.title: Each instrument answers a different question
lecture.say: Raise is for an error somebody else can handle: a caller passed a width of 1 to a function that draws boxes. Assert is for a belief of the programmer: if this list is sorted, the first item is not larger than the last, and if that is false the code is wrong and must stop. Logging is for a record: what did the program do, in what order, with which values. The debugger is for a question about state: what are the variables at exactly this line. The rest of the lecture takes them in that order and ends with three real bugs and the instrument that finds each.

lecture.title: Raise an exception when a call cannot be served
lecture.say: The function is the book’s box_print (Sweigart, 2025), with the calls that trigger each message. It checks its own arguments and raises an Exception with a message when one is wrong: a symbol that is not one character, a width or a height that is not greater than 2. The loop at the bottom calls it with a good box, a width of 1 and a two-character symbol. The except clause caught each exception, called it err and printed str(err), which is exactly the text given to raise. The caller can decide what to do.

lecture.title: An exception climbs the stack until something handles it
lecture.say: Nothing in read_age handles it, so the function is left; the same in load, and the same in process. Only the try around the call at the bottom has an except clause that matches, so it is caught there and execution continues with the print. The transcript is the proof: caught, then the message. This is why the chapter says a function should raise and let the caller who knows what to do handle it.

lecture.title: Read a traceback from the bottom up
lecture.say: The lines above go backwards through the calls that led there, so the frame just above the last line is where the exception was raised. Each frame has its file, its line number, its function and the source line itself.

lecture.title: Since Python 3.11: carets in tracebacks, notes on exceptions
lecture.say: Two additions since the book’s tracebacks. First, from Python 3.11 the traceback underlines the part of the line that failed. In print(data[‘a’][‘b’][‘c’]) the value at ‘b’ is None, so the third subscript fails, and the carets sit under it; before 3.11 you had to work that out yourself (Galindo Salgado et al., 2021). Second, an exception can carry notes: the program catches a ValueError, adds a note saying which field was being read, and re-raises; the note is kept in __notes__ and printed under the traceback if nobody handles it (Hatfield-Dodds, 2021). Neither is in the book; both are worth a sentence.

lecture.title: Predict first: does the program say the list is sorted?
lecture.say: Prediction first again. The list starts unsorted, is reversed instead of sorted, and the assert says the first item must not be larger than the last. Notice that an assert with no message raises AssertionError with an empty string as its message; the printed line shows repr(str(e)), which is two quotation marks with nothing between them.

lecture.title: User errors are handled; programmer errors are asserted
lecture.say: The distinction the chapter draws is the one to leave with. If the cause is outside your code, a missing file, bad input, a dropped connection, the program can do something sensible, so use exceptions and handle them. If the cause is a mistake in your code, there is nothing sensible to do except stop and fix it, and an assertion states the belief that turned out false.

lecture.title: An assertion can say why it failed
lecture.say: A bare assert tells you a check failed; adding a message tells you what the values were. The message is an expression after a comma and is evaluated only if the condition is false, so it costs nothing on the passing path.

lecture.title: Hazard: python -O removes every assert
lecture.say: Not in the book, and a genuine trap. The reference says the assert statement is equivalent to if __debug__: if not expression: raise AssertionError, and that no code is generated for it when optimisation is requested, as with the -O option (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The program shows both: compiled normally the assert raises and prints the message; compiled with optimize=1 the same source runs straight through to the print. So an assert is a development aid; anything the program depends on for correctness under all conditions must not be one.

lecture.title: What if print calls could be switched off with one line?
lecture.say: Everyone starts with print statements. They work, and they leave a mess: you must remember to remove them, and you cannot keep some and hide others. Logging solves exactly that problem.

lecture.title: basicConfig chooses the threshold, the format and the place
lecture.say: Three parts: the level says which messages to show, the format says what each line looks like, and the destination is the screen unless you give a file name.

lecture.title: Five levels, each with a number
lecture.say: The chapter’s five levels, lowest to highest importance: DEBUG for the detail you want while developing, INFO for confirmation that things work, WARNING for something unexpected, ERROR for a failure, CRITICAL for one that may stop the program. The threshold is a number, so the rule is simply: shown when the message’s number is at least the threshold’s.

lecture.title: Choose a threshold, see what is shown
lecture.say: This grid is a simulation you can also run yourself on the page. Every cell is what a real subprocess printed: for each setting the same five logging calls were run under Python 3.14.4 and the output lines were read back. Column one has no basicConfig at all and shows a surprise, taken up next. Columns two to six are the five thresholds; watch the shown cells shrink as the threshold rises. The last column is the disable function, which silences everything at or below the level it is given.

lecture.title: Why does logging.debug print nothing?
lecture.say: The commonest surprise for a beginner: they add logging.debug calls and see nothing. Debug and info are dropped.

lecture.title: Hazard: a second basicConfig call is ignored
lecture.say: Not in the book and a frequent puzzle in notebooks and tests, where something else has already configured logging. The program calls basicConfig with INFO, then again with DEBUG; the debug call after the second setup prints nothing, because the second call was ignored. The third call passes force=True, and now the debug message appears. The logging documentation says basicConfig does nothing if the root logger already has handlers configured unless force is given (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

lecture.title: Log to a file instead of the screen
lecture.say: The chapter writes to myProgramLog.txt; this program does the same in a temporary folder so it can be re-run anywhere, then reads the file back and prints it. Two messages were logged and both appear, because the threshold was DEBUG. Nothing was printed to the screen by the logging calls themselves: the record lives in the file (Sweigart, 2025).

lecture.title: Switch every message off with one line
lecture.say: This is the answer to the hook. Print calls have to be found and deleted; log calls are silenced by one line. In the real run, the critical message before the disable call appears, the two calls after it print nothing, and after logging.disable(logging.NOTSET) errors show again (Sweigart, 2025; Python Software Foundation, 2026).

lecture.title: Give the arguments to the call, not to an f-string
lecture.say: A practical point the book does not make. The level here is INFO, so the debug calls are not emitted. In the first call the object is passed as an argument and the logging module only converts it to text if the message will be shown, so its __str__ ran zero times. In the second the f-string builds the text before the call, so the conversion ran once even though nothing was logged. For a cheap value it does not matter; for an expensive one it does, and the logging HOWTO’s own example makes that point (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

lecture.title: Log messages are for the programmer; print is for the user
lecture.say: The chapter’s practice question 8 asks why logging is better than print for the same message, and its answer is about audience: log messages are for the programmer; messages the user should see, such as file not found or invalid input, use print (Sweigart, 2025).

lecture.title: Predict first: what does factorial(3) return?
lecture.say: The debug lines are what make the bug visible without a debugger: you can see the first pass multiply by zero.

lecture.title: Trace it: the first pass multiplies by zero
lecture.say: A trace table is how you reason about a loop without running it. Pass one: i is 0, so total times 0 is 0. From then on total stays 0, whatever i is, because anything times zero is zero. The last row also shows the debug line that closes the function and the value that print shows.

lecture.title: The fix is one line, and the log proves it
lecture.say: Same program with range(1, n + 1). The log now shows i is 1 and total is 1, then 2, then 6, and the call prints 6. Notice how the logging calls stayed in place while the fix went in; when the program is finished you raise the threshold or call disable and they fall silent, rather than deleting them (Sweigart, 2025).

lecture.title: What if you could freeze the program on one line and look around?
lecture.say: Logging tells you what happened. That is what a debugger is. The book’s chapter uses the debugger in the Mu editor (Sweigart, 2025); the controls have the same names in most editors, and the standard library has one of its own, which is the last part of this chapter.

lecture.title: Five controls, and a breakpoint to start from
lecture.say: Continue runs until it reaches a breakpoint or the end. Step In executes the next line and, if the line calls a function, goes inside it. Step Over executes the next line, running any function it calls at full speed without stopping inside. Step Out runs the rest of the current function and stops when it returns (Sweigart, 2025). Stop ends the program. Under each is the command of the standard library’s debugger, pdb, that does the same job: continue, step, next and return; the page’s simulator has all five buttons.

lecture.title: Continue runs to the next breakpoint
lecture.say: Both panels are frames from one recorded run of this program under Python 3.14.4: a line event stream, with the variables and the call stack at each stop. There is a breakpoint, the red dot, on line 7. This is the same simulator you get on the page, where you can set your own breakpoints by clicking a line number.

lecture.title: Step In goes inside a call; Step Over runs it whole
lecture.say: Three frames from the recorded run. Use Step In when you suspect the function you are calling; Step Over when you trust it and want to move on (Sweigart, 2025).

lecture.title: Step Out finishes this function and stops in its caller
lecture.say: The third stepping control. The debugger is stopped at line 2, inside add, with a and b set and three frames on the call stack. Step Out runs the rest of add and stops as soon as it returns, here at line 7 of main, with the call stack back to two frames (Sweigart, 2025). It is the way back after a Step In that turned out to be uninteresting.

lecture.title: Any Python has a debugger: breakpoint() and pdb
lecture.say: Not in the book, which uses an editor’s debugger, but this is the tool every Python installation has. Since Python 3.7 a call to breakpoint() pauses the program in the debugger at that line; it calls sys.breakpointhook, and setting the environment variable PYTHONBREAKPOINT to 0 makes the call do nothing, so you can leave one in and switch it off (Warsaw, 2017; Python Software Foundation, 2026). New in Python 3.14: the debugger can attach to a process that is already running, by its process identifier, using sys.remote_exec (Galindo Salgado, Wozniski and Stojanovic, 2024); the second line confirms that this build has it.

lecture.title: Worked case: the sum that prints 5342
lecture.say: The book’s buggy adding program: input() returns strings, so adding first, second and third joins the text and prints The sum is 5342 (Sweigart, 2025). In the debugger’s variable pane the values would show with quotation marks, which is the clue that they are strings and not numbers. Both transcripts are real runs of these programs with the inputs 5, 3 and 42.

lecture.title: Worked case: a guess that can never be right
lecture.say: The practice program in the chapter, cut down to the comparison that is wrong. random.randint(0, 1) gives an integer, the guess from input() is a string, and toss == guess compares the two, so it is always false. The seed is fixed, so the toss is heads in both runs: the run that guessed heads should have won, and it says Nope. The last line prints the two types.

lecture.title: What you can do now
lecture.say: Close the loop on the hook: the program runs and prints a wrong answer. Start by asking what you believe, and assert it. Add logging where you cannot tell what happened. Reach for the debugger when the state at one line is the question. Read every traceback from the bottom. Those four verbs are the chapter’s learning objectives on the interactive page.

lecture.title: Check yourself
lecture.say: Questions 1 to 3 revisit the assertion and logging material; question 4 the debugger controls from the book’s practice questions; question 5 the bug that ran through the chapter.
